The White-winged shrike-tanager (Lanio versicolor) is a passerine species inhabiting the understory of lowland forests in the southern Amazon basin. Field studies on a breeding population in southeastern Peru have documented that eggs are deposited in open-cup nests and subjected to a protracted incubation period. When incubated at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the developmental period culminates in hatching after approximately 15 days [ab = approximately 15 days]. The altricial nestlings emerge completely naked and with closed eyes, entirely dependent on both parents for thermoregulation and food delivery. Their body mass at the moment of hatching is remarkably low, averaging just 2 grams [Wwb = 2 grams], a value consistent with the pattern observed in other small-bodied tanagers. This minimal initial investment at birth is compensated by a rapid growth trajectory fueled by frequent provisioning visits, which allow the chick to increase its mass by nearly an order of magnitude before it reaches the nest-leaving stage. The specific timing of these early developmental events was measured using automated nest cameras and daily weighing protocols during two consecutive breeding seasons.

Under the typical ambient conditions of the breeding season, during which daytime body temperatures of active adults frequently reach 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the nestlings achieve several critical milestones in rapid succession. Fledging, defined as the point at which the juvenile leaves the nest for the first time and sustains brief flights, occurs at 11 days after hatching [tx = 11 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively short nestling period is characteristic of many tropical passerines and is thought to reduce the risk of nest predation, which is a primary source of mortality in this system. Once the young bird has departed the nest, it enters a dependent post-fledging phase during which the parents continue to supply food, though the fledgling increasingly forages on its own. The capacity for sustained flight and effective evasion of predators improves markedly within a few days of nest departure. These developmental transitions are tightly synchronized with the phenology of arthropod prey abundance in the forest understory, which peaks during the early wet season when most nesting attempts are initiated.

Sexual maturation in this species proceeds steadily following the fledgling period, culminating in the attainment of full reproductive competency. Under the thermoregulatory conditions typical of the active adult state at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], puberty, defined by the onset of functional gametogenesis and the development of adult plumage, is reached at 33 days since birth [tp = 33 days since birth]. This represents a fairly rapid progression to physiological maturity for a bird of its body size, likely an adaptation to the high rates of adult turnover driven by intense predation pressure in its Amazonian habitat. Following puberty, individuals typically undergo a period of social maturation during which they establish territories and form pair bonds. The time since birth at first brood, marking the age at which a female lays her first clutch of eggs, occurs roughly one year later, at approximately 365 days since birth [tR = approximately 365 days since birth] under the same active thermal regime at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This delay between puberty and first reproduction reflects the challenges of territory acquisition and mate attraction in a saturated environment.

Adult body mass in the White-winged shrike-tanager is sexually monomorphic, with both males and females reaching a final, asymptotic mass after completing their post-juvenile molt. The ultimate wet weight attained by breeding adults averages approximately 20 grams [Wwi = approximately 20 grams], a figure that places the species among the mid-sized members of the Thraupidae family. This body mass is maintained with only minor seasonal fluctuations, rarely varying by more than one gram between the dry and wet seasons. The relatively small size of this bird imposes significant constraints on its life history, including high mass-specific metabolic rates and a corresponding need for frequent foraging bouts to meet daily energy demands. Adult individuals are primarily insectivorous but supplement their diet with small fruits, and their foraging strategy involves active gleaning of insects from foliage and bark in the middle forest strata. The consistency of adult body mass across populations suggests that food resources are generally not limiting for established territorial adults in these Amazonian forests.

Reproductive output in Lanio versicolor is characterized by a relatively modest annual investment. Females produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = a single clutch each year], with each clutch containing exactly 2 eggs [N_R_i = 2 eggs]. This combination of a single, small clutch annually defines a slow life-history pace compared to many temperate passerines, which frequently produce multiple broods per season. At 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the maximum reproduction rate is 2 eggs per year [Ri = 2 eggs per year]. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species under field conditions, based on re-sightings of color-banded individuals, is approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This longevity is notable for a bird of only 20 grams, as small-bodied tropical passerines often exhibit extended lifespans relative to their temperate counterparts, a pattern attributed to lower extrinsic mortality rates in environments where predation is seasonally predictable and food resources are relatively stable. The interplay between a low reproductive rate and a long potential lifespan suggests that adult survival is a critical demographic parameter for population persistence, and any factor that elevates adult mortality is likely to have pronounced negative effects on population growth.
